social-issues-human-rights.explanation: Simply dropping the supplier doesn't fulfil due diligence obligations — the expectation (under CSDDD, the UNGPs, and the OECD Guidelines) is to investigate, use leverage to fix the problem, and remediate harm already done, not just walk away.

social-issues-human-rights.question: An employee in a low-cost country is paid the legal minimum wage. Is that automatically sufficient under modern ESG expectations?
options: No, because ESG expectations require paying the minimum wage of the company's home country
Yes, because ESG standards never go beyond what the law requires
Yes, as long as the company discloses the wage in its ESRS S1 report
Not necessarily — a living wage benchmark can sit well above the legal minimum
social-issues-human-rights.explanation: Legal compliance and a living wage are two different bars. A worker can be paid entirely legally and still fall short of what a living wage benchmark considers a decent standard of living.

csr-ethics.question: An employee wants to report suspected fraud but is worried about retaliation. What should your company already have in place?
options: A social audit of the finance department
An anonymous suggestion box, which on its own satisfies the Whistleblower Directive
A protected whistleblower reporting channel, as required under the Whistleblower Directive
A grievance mechanism specifically for external communities only
csr-ethics.explanation: The Whistleblower Directive requires companies to provide a protected reporting channel and shields whistleblowers from retaliation — an employee shouldn't have to choose between staying silent and risking their job.

csr-ethics.question: A company donates generously to charity but has weak labour practices in its own supply chain. Which CSR framework best explains why this isn't enough?
options: Carroll's CSR pyramid: economic and legal duties come before philanthropy
Triple bottom line, which lets strong philanthropy offset weak labour practices
Shared value theory, which says charitable giving is the main way to create social value
The EU Taxonomy's minimum safeguards for aligned activities
csr-ethics.explanation: Carroll's pyramid stacks responsibilities: economic and legal first, then ethical, with philanthropic at the top. A company can't paper over weak ethical/legal conduct in its own operations with generosity elsewhere.

governance-anti-corruption.question: A board is entirely made up of executives with no independent oversight. What governance concern does this raise?
options: A concern only for listed companies, since unlisted companies are exempt from board-independence expectations
It automatically breaches the EU Taxonomy's governance rules
It only matters under two-tier board structures
Weak tone at the top and no independent check
governance-anti-corruption.explanation: Independent oversight is exactly what keeps 'tone at the top' honest — a board with no independent voices has a much weaker check against poor decisions or misconduct going unchallenged.

governance-anti-corruption.question: Shareholders vote against a proposed executive bonus at the AGM (annual general meeting), but the board pays it anyway. What mechanism did the board just override?
options: Lobbying transparency
Stewardship
Say-on-climate
Say-on-pay
governance-anti-corruption.explanation: Say-on-pay is shareholders' formal vote on executive remuneration — overriding a losing vote undermines the entire point of the mechanism, even where it isn't always legally binding.

gri-standards.question: A company already reports under GRI. Does that mean it's automatically compliant with CSRD?
options: Yes, as long as it applies the GRI Universal Standards in full
No: ESRS has its own mandatory requirements that GRI doesn't fully cover
No, because CSRD only accepts reports prepared by the company's statutory auditor
Yes, because the EU legally recognises GRI as equivalent
gri-standards.explanation: GRI-ESRS interoperability reduces duplicate work, but it doesn't make the two identical — a GRI reporter still has real additional work to do to meet CSRD's own mandatory ESRS structure.

gri-standards.question: A company wants to claim its report is 'in accordance with GRI.' What does that specifically require?
options: Meeting every requirement of the GRI Universal Standards
Having the report audited under CSRD's limited assurance
Referring to GRI in the report's methodology section
Publishing a content index and reporting only its three highest-ranked topics, even if other topics are also material
gri-standards.explanation: 'In accordance with GRI' is a specific, checkable claim — it requires meeting every Universal Standards requirement, not just loosely referencing GRI somewhere in the document.

other-reporting-standards.question: An investor asks for the company's TCFD-aligned climate disclosure. The company has only published a GRI report. Is that sufficient?
options: Yes, because IFRS S2 has replaced TCFD entirely
No, because TCFD was fully discontinued and can't be used any more
Not necessarily: TCFD's structure and scenario analysis differ from GRI's format
Yes, because the emissions standard in GRI already contains every scenario analysis requirement of TCFD
other-reporting-standards.explanation: TCFD (and IFRS S2, built on it) asks for a specific structure — including scenario analysis — that a GRI report doesn't automatically provide. The investor's ask likely isn't met by the GRI report alone.

other-reporting-standards.question: A company is deciding whether to adopt IFRS S1/S2 or ESRS as its primary sustainability reporting standard. What's the key difference to weigh?
options: IFRS S1/S2 covers only climate, while ESRS also covers social and governance topics
ESRS applies financial materiality, while IFRS S1/S2 applies double materiality
ESRS is voluntary for EU companies, while IFRS S1/S2 is mandatory in the EU
IFRS S1/S2 applies financial (single) materiality; ESRS applies double materiality
other-reporting-standards.explanation: The materiality lens is the key divide: IFRS S1/S2 is built for global investors and financial materiality; ESRS is built for the EU's double materiality approach, covering impact as well as financial relevance.

csddd.question: A tier-2 supplier (a supplier of your direct supplier) is flagged for environmental violations. Is that outside your company's CSDDD responsibility since it's not a direct contract?
options: Yes: CSDDD only covers your direct, tier-1 suppliers
No: it extends across the value chain, including tier-2 suppliers
No, but only for CSRD reporting purposes, not under CSDDD
Yes, unless the violation is also a criminal offence in the supplier's country
csddd.explanation: CSDDD's due diligence obligation covers the value chain broadly, not just direct contracts — risk prioritisation is how a company decides where to focus first, not an excuse to ignore tier-2+ risk entirely.

csddd.question: Your company discovers it has contributed to a serious human rights violation at a supplier. What does CSDDD's due diligence obligation require beyond simply ending the contract?
options: Nothing further: termination is always sufficient
Filing a report with the OECD national contact point
Remediation: addressing the harm already caused
Paying a fixed fine to the supervisory authority before any other step
csddd.explanation: Due diligence isn't satisfied by walking away — where the company caused or contributed to the harm, CSDDD's cycle requires remediation, actually addressing the harm done, not just cutting ties. (Where a supplier caused the harm entirely alone, the company must instead use its leverage to push for remediation.)

sfdr.question: A fund manager wants to market a new fund as Article 9 to attract sustainability-focused investors, even though its holdings include companies with no clear sustainability objective. What's the risk?
options: Investors could claim compensation automatically, because Article 9 is a legally protected label
None, as long as the fund also publishes its principal adverse impacts
The fund would automatically be reclassified as Article 6
Greenwashing risk: its holdings may not meet Article 9's definition
sfdr.explanation: Article 9's definition of sustainable investment is specific and testable — mismarketing a fund that doesn't actually meet it is exactly the kind of financial-sector greenwashing risk SFDR (and its enforcement) targets.

sfdr.question: An investor asks why a fund's PAI (Principal Adverse Impacts) disclosure shows a high carbon footprint, even though the fund is marketed as sustainable. What should the investor understand?
options: A high PAI figure proves the fund is not genuinely sustainable
A high PAI figure means the fund has breached its commitments as an Article 8 product
PAI exists to show a fund's downsides, not just its positives
PAI disclosure is only required for Article 9 funds, so this fund must be Article 9
sfdr.explanation: PAI disclosure exists precisely so a fund's negative impacts can't be hidden behind its positive marketing — a sustainability-labelled fund can still carry real adverse impacts worth scrutinising.

eu-taxonomy.question: A company's activity contributes substantially to climate mitigation but causes serious harm to local biodiversity. Does it qualify as Taxonomy-aligned?
options: No: DNSH means it must not seriously harm other objectives, including biodiversity
Yes, since climate mitigation is the most important objective
Yes, if the harm is offset by a larger contribution to another environmental objective
Yes, as long as the activity is taxonomy-eligible
eu-taxonomy.explanation: Substantial contribution to one objective is only half the test — DNSH means serious harm to any of the other five objectives, including biodiversity, disqualifies the activity from being Taxonomy-aligned.

eu-taxonomy.question: A company reports that 60% of its turnover is 'taxonomy-eligible.' A journalist asks if that means 60% is genuinely sustainable. What's the accurate answer?
options: Yes, because once a company publishes a transition plan its eligible share counts as aligned
No, because eligibility is measured on capital and operating expenditure only, never on turnover
No: eligible only means covered; aligned means meeting every criterion
Yes, 'eligible' and 'aligned' mean the same thing here
eu-taxonomy.explanation: Eligible just means the activity is on the Taxonomy's list at all — it says nothing about whether it actually meets the substantial contribution, DNSH, and minimum safeguards tests that alignment requires.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.question: A company issues a bond marketed as a 'green bond,' but the proceeds go into the company's general operating budget rather than any specific environmental project. Is this consistent with the Green Bond Principles?
options: No — green bonds are specifically defined by proceeds being earmarked for environmental projects
Yes, as long as the company publishes a sustainability report in the same year
This only matters for the EU Green Bond Standard, not ICMA's principles
Yes, as long as the company is in a green sector
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.explanation: A green bond's defining feature is earmarked use of proceeds — funding general operations instead of specific environmental projects breaks the core premise the Green Bond Principles are built around.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.question: An analyst notices that a company's MSCI ESG rating and its Sustainalytics score seem to send opposite signals. What's the most likely explanation?
options: MSCI rates ESG risk, while Sustainalytics rates a company's financial performance
Both ratings use the same method, so one of them must contain an error
Rating divergence: agencies use different methodologies and score differently
MSCI compares a company with its own past, Sustainalytics with its industry peers
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.explanation: Rating divergence is a well-documented, structural feature of the ESG ratings industry — different agencies weigh different factors differently, so genuinely different scores for the same company aren't unusual.

greenwashing-empco-ucpd.question: Marketing wants to advertise a product as 'environmentally friendly.' What is the main ESG risk in using that phrase as-is?
options: A generic environmental claim: the company must be able to show recognised excellent environmental performance that supports the claim
The claim is only a risk if the product also carries an environmental label
An internal lifecycle study is enough on its own, even without recognised excellent environmental performance
The claim is only a risk when it is used to compare the product with a competitor's
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.explanation: 'Environmentally friendly' with no evidence behind it is a textbook generic environmental claim — EmpCo specifically bans this kind of vague language unless the company can demonstrate recognised excellent environmental performance, in practice usually via the EU Ecolabel or an equivalent recognised ecolabelling scheme, not just general supporting data.

greenwashing-empco-ucpd.question: A company quietly makes real progress on emissions but stops mentioning it publicly, worried any claim might trigger scrutiny. What's this behaviour called, and is it actually the safe choice?
options: Greenwashing: it's just as risky as overclaiming
Substantiation: this is the correct, required approach
Greenhushing: it avoids greenwashing risk, but real progress goes uncommunicated
Comparative environmental claims: a form of misleading comparison
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.explanation: Greenhushing is a real, if underappreciated, side effect of tighter claims rules — it isn't illegal, but it does mean investors, customers, and regulators lose visibility into genuine progress a company is actually making.

key-players-institutions.question: A colleague conflates MSCI's ESG rating with a regulatory requirement, saying 'we need a good MSCI score to comply with CSRD.' What's the error?
options: MSCI is a private rating agency, not a regulator
ESMA accepts an MSCI score as proof of CSRD compliance
MSCI is a standard-setter whose standards are voluntary under CSRD
CSRD only recognises ratings from agencies registered with EFRAG
key-players-institutions.explanation: MSCI ESG Research is a private ratings provider used by investors — it has no formal role in determining CSRD compliance, which is a separate, EU regulatory requirement entirely distinct from any commercial rating.

key-players-institutions.question: A supplier proudly shows an EcoVadis Bronze medal as proof of full ESG compliance. What should you keep in mind before accepting that at face value?
options: Bronze means the supplier has passed an independent on-site audit
EcoVadis medals are only awarded to suppliers of listed companies
EcoVadis only assesses environmental performance, not social topics
Bronze is the lowest medal: baseline performance, not full compliance
key-players-institutions.explanation: EcoVadis medals run Bronze through Platinum — Bronze is a real but modest result, useful context rather than a guarantee of full compliance across every ESG dimension a buyer might care about.

timeline-milestones.question: A colleague claims CSRD's reporting requirements have stayed exactly the same since it was adopted in 2022. What should you correct them on?
options: The 2026 Omnibus reform narrowed CSRD's scope and simplified ESRS
The 2026 Omnibus reform only postponed start dates and left scope and standards unchanged
CSRD was adopted in 2022, but the ESRS were replaced by the GRI Standards
CSRD was extended in 2026 to cover all listed SMEs
timeline-milestones.explanation: The 2026 Omnibus reform is a real, substantial change — the revised ESRS adopted in July 2026 cut mandatory datapoints by more than 60% and narrowed CSRD's scope. Treating the 2022 text as still fully current is a common but outdated assumption.

timeline-milestones.question: A colleague asks why CSDDD's timeline changed from a staggered rollout to one single date. What happened?
options: The 2026 Omnibus reform replaced the waves with a single date
The single date was chosen by each member state for its own companies
The staggered rollout was cancelled by the EU Court of Justice
The change only moved the deadline for the largest companies and kept the later waves
timeline-milestones.explanation: This is a direct, concrete effect of the 2026 Omnibus reform — instead of tracking which 'wave' a company fell into, everyone in scope now works toward the same single 2029 deadline.

csrd-esrs.question: Your company's carbon emissions barely move the needle on your financial statements, but they visibly affect air quality in the town where your factory sits. Does ESRS require you to report on them?
options: No: if a topic isn't financially material, ESRS doesn't require disclosure
Yes: a topic is reportable if it is material financially or for its impact
Only if residents of the town have filed a formal complaint against the company
No: ESRS only assesses financial materiality; impact materiality was dropped in the Omnibus reform
csrd-esrs.explanation: Double materiality means a topic can require disclosure for either reason on its own — its effect on the company's finances, or the company's effect on people and the planet. Local air-quality impact is a textbook impact-materiality case, independent of whether it shows up on the balance sheet.

csrd-esrs.question: A standalone EU company has an average of 600 employees and annual net turnover of €300 million. Does it meet the general post-Omnibus CSRD size thresholds?
options: Yes, any company with over 250 employees was always in scope
No: scope now needs over 1,000 employees and over €450 million in net turnover
Yes, because it counts as a large unlisted company
Yes: scope needs over 500 employees and over €250 million in net turnover
csrd-esrs.explanation: The 2026 Omnibus reform narrowed mandatory CSRD scope to companies exceeding both 1,000 employees and €450 million in turnover. A company below both thresholds has no mandatory CSRD obligation, even though it would have been in scope under the original, much broader 2022 text.

esg-ratings-data-providers.question: A retailer wants its suppliers to upload one social audit report and choose which customers can see it, instead of repeating audits for each buyer. Which service is built for this?
options: EcoVadis
Sedex
CDP (formerly the Carbon Disclosure Project)
RepRisk
esg-ratings-data-providers.explanation: Sedex lets suppliers upload audit reports once and choose which customers can see them. EcoVadis scores suppliers, CDP scores environmental disclosures and RepRisk tracks incidents. None of those is built for sharing audit reports.

esg-ratings-data-providers.question: Two providers rate the same bank very differently: one gives a strong grade, the other a weak one. What is the most useful first step?
options: Assume the lower rating is correct, because it is more cautious
Average the two scores and treat the result as the true rating
Prefer the provider that covers the most banks
Check what each rating measures and where its data comes from
esg-ratings-data-providers.explanation: Providers can measure different things and use different data. Comparing their methods helps explain why the same bank gets different ratings.

regulatoryMilestones.title: CBAM definitive period begins
regulatoryMilestones.description: The transitional reporting-only phase ends and the real obligation starts: importers must declare embedded emissions on covered goods and buy CBAM certificates, with the first certificate sales opening 1 February 2027.

regulatoryMilestones.title: EU Taxonomy revised Delegated Act entered into force
regulatoryMilestones.description: A 10% materiality threshold now lets companies skip assessing minor activities, cutting required datapoints by roughly 64% for non-financial companies.

regulatoryMilestones.title: Omnibus I Directive entered into force
regulatoryMilestones.description: The reform that narrowed CSRD's scope and removed CSDDD's EU-wide civil liability regime and mandatory transition-plan obligation officially took effect.

regulatoryMilestones.title: EU ESG Ratings Regulation applies
regulatoryMilestones.description: The rules apply from 2 July 2026. ESMA supervises the ESG rating providers covered by the regulation, and transitional rules apply to providers already active in the EU.

regulatoryMilestones.title: EmpCo Directive becomes applicable
regulatoryMilestones.description: EU member states were due to apply their national rules from this date. The rules ban generic environmental claims without recognised excellent environmental performance relevant to the claim. They also ban claims that offsetting makes a product's greenhouse gas impact neutral, lower or positive.

regulatoryMilestones.title: Revised ESRS entered into force
regulatoryMilestones.description: The simplified reporting standards, published in the Official Journal on 21 September 2026, entered into force. They apply to financial years starting on or after 1 January 2027.

regulatoryMilestones.title: EUDR applies to large and medium operators
regulatoryMilestones.description: The EU Deforestation Regulation starts applying to large and medium operators — twice postponed from its original 30 December 2024 date. Micro and small operators get until 30 June 2027, except for products already covered by the EU Timber Regulation.

regulatoryMilestones.title: Revised ESRS starts applying
regulatoryMilestones.description: Companies begin reporting financial year 2027 under the simplified ESRS (more than 60% fewer mandatory datapoints). Companies already reporting under ESRS may use the revised standards earlier, for financial years starting in 2026.

regulatoryMilestones.title: CSRD Wave 2 starts applying
regulatoryMilestones.description: Companies not yet reporting that have more than 1,000 employees and more than €450m net turnover start with financial year 2027. Those with a calendar financial year publish their first report in 2028.

regulatoryMilestones.title: CBAM certificate sales open
regulatoryMilestones.description: Importers can start buying CBAM certificates to cover the emissions of goods imported in 2026.

regulatoryMilestones.title: First CBAM declaration due
regulatoryMilestones.description: Importers must submit their first annual CBAM declaration and surrender certificates for 2026 imports.

regulatoryMilestones.title: EU Forced Labour Regulation applies
regulatoryMilestones.description: Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 becomes directly applicable across all member states, banning any product made with forced labour from being placed on, sold in, or exported from the EU market.

regulatoryMilestones.title: CSDDD transposition deadline
regulatoryMilestones.description: EU member states' deadline to write CSDDD's Omnibus-revised rules into national law — exactly one year before the directive actually starts applying to companies.

regulatoryMilestones.title: CSDDD applies to all in-scope companies
regulatoryMilestones.description: The single application date replacing the originally staggered rollout — every in-scope company, regardless of size tier, is covered from this date. The annual reporting duty under Article 16 follows for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2030.
